title: New menopause guidelines designed to cut through misinformation
text:
Hot Flushes. Night sweats. Vaginal dryness. Painful sex. A frequent need to wee.

Menopause marks the end of a woman's reproductive years and is associated with a range of symptoms that can affect their quality of life.

There's a lot of information and misinformation about the best treatments to help ease the severity of symptoms.

In a bid to make things easier, the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) has developed a new set of clinical guidelines.

Loading...

The guidelines clarify when to use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) over other medicines and what options are available for those with a history of breast cancer.

RANZCOG guideline development group chair Catriona Melville said they wanted to "cut through the noise" and provide clear, evidence-based recommendations for clinicians to discuss with their patients.

"If your clinician is not clear about where the evidence lies and what's safe and what isn't safe, and what's recommended and what isn't recommended, then they're not in a position to have that patient-centred discussion about what the available [treatment] options are," she said.

What do the guidelines cover?

The new guidelines provide evidence-based advice for managing the symptoms of menopause, which begins 12 months after a woman's last period.

The guidelines cover vasomotor symptoms (such as hot flushes and night sweats) and genito-urinary symptoms (such as vaginal dryness and the frequent need to urinate) of menopause in women 40 years and above.

They do not cover the management of bone density, joint pain, libido, depression or anxiety.

Experts sceptical about menopause 'cliff-like' decline A new international study suggests menopause-related changes to the body are sudden and "cliff-like", but Australian experts urge caution interpreting the results.

Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said not all women experienced the same type or severity of symptoms.

While she was not involved in developing the guidelines, she said they reinforced the need for clinicians to treat the whole person in front of them, not just the symptom.

"We should also be looking at lifestyle and other risk factors around the time of the menopause," Dr Simonis said.

"This is a really important time to talk about [cholesterol] lipid control, bone density management and lifestyle activities.

"Looking at family history of other cancers, breast screening, cervical screening and having that conversation around chronic conditions."

How do the guidelines work?

The guidelines list a range of possible treatment options for different menopausal symptoms, including menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), acupuncture and hypnosis, ranking available evidence on a scale of very low to high.

The guidelines recommend that women taking MHT have an annual review with their doctor.

But there's not enough evidence that weight loss or physical activity alone will improve hot flushes or night sweats, or that hypnosis will improve sleep.

Dr Melville, a specialist gynaecologist and sub-specialist in sexual and reproductive health, said the new guidelines would hopefully make it easier for clinicians and patients to understand their options.

For example, women with a history of breast cancer can be offered vaginal oestrogen to ease menopausal symptoms.

Although RANZCOG had previously released statements about managing menopausal symptoms, Dr Melville said these were their first evidence-based guidelines.

How will it improve patient care?

Women should receive the same standardised recommendations no matter who they see or where they live if clinicians across Australia use the same guidelines.

Women cut HRT patches in half amid ongoing shortage Supplies of some HRT patches may not return to normal until at least the end of the year.

Jean Hailes for Women's Health chief executive Sarah White, who was not involved with the guidelines, said this was important because clinicians wanted to give their patients the very best support, but there was a lot of online misinformation to wade through.

"It really will help the health professional to have these new guidelines sitting in front of them so that they can talk them through and reassure women that they are getting the very best advice," she said.

The guidelines also encourage clinicians to ask women approaching menopause if they experience any "troublesome" symptoms, especially if patients are First Nations, Māori and Pacific Islander women and others who may experience barriers to treatment.

This will make it easier for women to get help, even if they find it hard to ask.

Won't there be new national guidelines soon?

The Australian government has funded separate perimenopause and menopause guidelines expected to be released next year.

These guidelines, which RANZCOG is contributing to, will be continually updated as new evidence emerges.

Dr Simonis welcomed the spotlight on the health of menopausal women.

She encouraged anyone experiencing troublesome symptoms to book an appointment with their GP and advised women approaching mid-life to schedule a check-up.

"Menopause is not a stage to be afraid of or to dread; it's a natural phase of life," she said.

title: Wildfires rage in Southern California, burn homes
text:
Firefighters in Southern California say a fast-moving wildfire has ripped through at least six homes, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.

TV footage showed homes engulfed in flames in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County on Friday, local time.

Firefighters doused two-storey suburban homes with flames leaping out of their roofs. Black smoke billowed over tennis courts and backyard swimming pools.

Over 500 firefighters were battling the blaze that had grown to nearly 2 square kilometres, said Captain Steve Concialdi, a spokesman with the Orange County Fire Authority.

A firefighter works to douse a blaze in San Juan Capistrano. (AP: Jae C. Hong)

"We're doing everything we can to protect structures," he told KTLA-TV.

An evacuation shelter has opened in each city.

The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano.

It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast.

The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night.

Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off.

A separate fire shut down a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego, adding hours to commutes throughout Southern California.

The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides.

San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and is popular with beachgoers and surfers.

A resident grabs a garden hose in an effort to help with a wildfire spreading in his neighbourhood, in San Juan Capistrano. (AP: Jae C. Hong)

Thousands were being asked to evacuate, said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente council member.

"The fire is right up on the city," he said.

"It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."

Nine schools were also closed on Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.

Howard Hart, a local council member, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated on Friday with a to-go bag.

Laura Hart has not had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she has lived in the community, she said.

"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said.

"We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."

Santa Ana winds hit

The Bryson Fire that sparked on Thursday, local time, in Malibu had died down significantly by Friday and firefighters were focused on mop-up and containment, officials said.

The blaze prompted evacuation orders and warnings for a swath of the Santa Monica Mountains that covered more than 12,000 people.

Winds from 32km/h to 56km/h were expected on Friday, with gusts forecast to reach 80km/h to 112km/h in some areas, the National Weather Service said.

A firefighting helicopter drops water as the Bryson Fire, burns in the hills east of Malibu. (Reuters: David Swanson)

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city's response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds.

The fire department also asked for help from the state's Office of Emergency Services.

"It's a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert," said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.

In some areas temperatures soared as high as 38 degrees Celsius.

The weather authority said fire danger would remain through much of Saturday, warning residents to be prepared for emergency evacuations.

They also cautioned drivers about dangerous crosswinds, particularly on elevated roadways.

Firefighters battle several blazes

Firefighters on Friday worked to contain two other fires that erupted on Thursday afternoon and triggered evacuation orders in the city of Azusa, east of LA, and Camp Pendleton, near San Diego.

More than 200,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.

Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds.

Firefighters use water hoses in San Clemente. (Reuters: Caroline Brehman )

Farther south, a fire at the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton threatened buildings and doubled in size over one day to more than 8 square kilometres.

The blaze crossed containment lines on Friday morning, closing a section of the I-5 freeway as the fire burned steadily toward it.

Power cuts widespread

In Northern California, some communities in the Sierra Nevada and its foothills began experiencing strong winds, high temperatures and low humidity on Wednesday night.

The weather service issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California throughout Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

Such warnings are issued when weather conditions create an increased risk of wildfires.

Customers from the Central Coast to the upper corners of the Sierra Nevada could be without power through Saturday afternoon, Pacific Gas and Electric Company said.

AP/AFP

title: The humble chickpea has just boomed in value
text:
Australian chickpeas are in hot demand, with delivered prices surging this month towards $1,000 per tonne in some regions.

It is a significant jump from earlier in the year, when the market was trading closer to $600 per tonne.

Grains Australia Pulse Council chair Peter Wilson said it was a great result for growers.

"We haven't seen $1,000 per tonne since 2024, so it's significant. It's a great price," he said.

" For growers who have ended up with a decent [chickpea] crop, this is balance-sheet altering. There's no other way to describe it. "

Chickpea prices have gone up considerably this month. (ABC Landline)

What is driving the chickpea boom?

So what is driving the sudden price surge for Australian chickpeas?

Mr Wilson said it was due to a combination of factors.

"There's a lot of volatility globally right now, which is creating enormous turbulence in logistics and supply chains, which is keeping buyers on edge," he said.

"We're also seeing the impacts of El Niño, which looks to have left parts of India with lower-than-average rainfall from the monsoon, which has caused their local chickpea prices to rise, which is pushing everything along."

The season's first delivery of chickpeas to the Mt McLaren receival site in Queensland. (Supplied: Marc Johnston/GrainCorp)

Mr Wilson said there were several nations wanting to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan, which starts in early February.

"Ramadan creates peak demand for a lot of our pulse crops [like chickpeas], and we see buyers wanting to have product pre-positioned at least one month ahead of Ramadan," he said.

"So we're seeing some urgency from buyers trying to get product onboard vessels for key destination markets such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and the UAE, so it's in the market and ready for that Ramadan demand."

In its most recent crop forecast, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES) predicted Australian chickpea production would fall by 52 per cent "to just over 1 million tonnes in 2026–27" due to significant cuts to area planted and expected lower yields in the major growing regions of northern New South Wales and Queensland.

ABC Landline has been told that forecast may be "optimistic" and the overall crop might be even lower, which is another reason why there is some buyer urgency at the moment.

Prices are expected to ease as harvest supply increases.

New season chickpeas arrive at the receival site at Yamala, Queensland. (Supplied: Fred Smith/GrainCorp)

Cashing in

North West Queensland chickpea grower Lucas Findley said he was pleased with his harvest, yielding about 1.2 tonnes per hectare.

Although he had already forward-sold most of his chickpeas at a lower price, he said it was still exciting to see the market rally.

"High prices are always good for any commodity and I'm happy for anyone who can take full advantage of these prices," Mr Findley said.

"We'd sold around 75 per cent of our chickpea crop prior to this recent price rise at a good price that we were happy with.

"But we still have around 25 per cent of the crop available to take advantage of the stronger prices, which will be a very nice finish to the season."

Hummus is made from cooked, mashed chickpeas. (ABC News: Wesley Mitton)

Mr Findley grows about 1,300 hectares of chickpeas as part of his grain and cotton rotation in Julia Creek.

His chickpeas will be exported out of the Townsville Port, which is gearing up for its second-ever dry bulk shipment of the pulse.

Last October, more than 38,000 tonnes of chickpeas were sent to India and Pakistan in a first-of-its-kind shipment from north Queensland, sourced from growing regions including Richmond, Julia Creek, Maxwelton and Marathon.

This year, the port will also export sorghum for the first time, which Mr Findley said was "fantastic".

"It just shows that people are supporting the expansion of North West Queensland farming more and more," he said.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview.

title: SA health care worker banned after cancer cure claims
text:
A man who abused "vulnerable" clients by claiming he could cure cancer and make an non-ambulatory woman walk has failed in a bid to overturn his "indefinite" ban from practising as a health care worker.

Adrian Fabio Mangini was providing health services in South Australia, including "hypnogym", hypnotherapy and yoga, before he was banned from practising indefinitely in 2024 by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner.

A judgement published by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) earlier this year upheld the decision after Mr Mangini asked for a review.

It upheld the previous findings by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner which included Mr Mangini's claim, in a YouTube video, that he made a woman living with a non-ambulatory disability walk "after an 11-minute consultation where he hypnotised her and counselled her by providing encouraging words".

Senior member of SACAT Jacqueline Rugless also reiterated in her judgment that there was "no evidence" the woman "was previously disabled or that she could not walk at all or could only walk with a frame".

"I am satisfied that the applicant claimed in advertising or promotional materials to have made … 'a disabled person' walk as a direct result of his provision of services, in circumstances where there was and is still no proof that [she] was disabled and could not walk prior to the consultation," she said.

Cancer cure claims

The tribunal also upheld a previous finding that Mr Mangini had claimed he cured cancer.

"The applicant [Mr Mangini] privately messaged a client about assisting a different client of his to be 10 years' cancer free, such that he represented he was able to cure cancer," the judgement said.

The judgement also upheld a finding that the health care worker had "engaged in behaviour of a sexual or close personal nature with a client".

The South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal upheld a decision to ban Adrian Mangini from practising. (ABC News: Eugene Boisvert)

"I am satisfied that the proven conduct of the applicant demonstrates a degree of overt abuse of the health and safety of vulnerable consumers together with open and deliberate dishonesty in his advertising about the alleged beneficial consequences of the services he sought to offer to consumers," Ms Rugless said.

"The applicant has demonstrated no insight into his behaviour and has displayed no remorse for his conduct. I am satisfied that he continues to pose a risk to the public.

"The proven conduct is completely incompatible with Mr Mangini continuing to be a health care worker or a health services provider."

Proceedings labelled a 'vendetta'

The judgment also outlined that Mr Mangini had argued in the tribunal that the proceedings were brought against him because of a vendetta by the Community Services Complaints Commissioner.

"I am not satisfied that there is any evidence of a 'vendetta' against Mr Mangini by a person or persons either known to him or unknown, or of a racist motivation behind the allegations that were before the Commissioner," Ms Rugless said in the judgement.

"In any event I am satisfied that the allegations found proved in the Commissioner's report have been independently verified by the Commissioner's investigation."

Mr Mangini has filed an appeal against SACAT's decision in the state's Supreme Court.

title: Indigenous rockers record third album in outback shed
text:
It has been decades since the Spinifex people were forcefully moved off their ancestral lands for the Maralinga nuclear tests in the 1950s.

For Indigenous songwriter James (Jay) Minning, writing about those struggles while on country in Western Australia's Great Victoria Desert has provided something of a musical awakening.

"My people have been fighting for that land, to get it back, and that's what's made me really interested in the land and that's why I keep writing songs about our land," he said.

"Everything you write down ... it's good to get the message out there in rock 'n' roll."

The Desert Stars (from left) Desmond Anderson, Ashley Frances, Jay Minning and Justin Currie. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

Third album in works

Minning is the lead singer of outback four-piece The Desert Stars, which has just finished a dozen new tracks for the band's third album in what could be the most remote recording project in the world.

The band members grew up together at Cundalee and Tjuntjuntjarra, about 650 kilometres east of Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Since their 2003 self-titled debut album, The Desert Stars have toured extensively around the country, developing a cult following in remote communities.

An appearance in the 2022 documentary Gravel Road, which followed the band on one of its remote tours, also raised their profile.

Desert Stars lead singer James Minning and lead guitarist Desmond Anderson. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

With band members living between Tjuntjuntjarra and Kalgoorlie-Boulder, it can be difficult to get them together long enough to learn new songs.

But for a couple of weeks in September, the band gathered in Ilkurlka to lay down tracks for the third album, due out sometime next year.

The remote outpost is a lifeline for outback travellers along the Anne Beadell Highway, an unsealed track stretching 1,300km between Laverton, WA and Cooper Pedy, South Australia.

It is widely considered to be Australia's most isolated roadhouse.

"It's remote, no-one's there, only the sound of nature and it's the way we like it to get the raw sound of it," Minning said.

"It's healing being out there, you're healed and you're ready to go."

The Desert Stars recording in a shed in the remote community of Ilkurlka in WA. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

Recording in a shed

Tamworth-based musician and producer Leigh Ivin has been recording The Desert Stars in between stints managing the Ilkurka Roadhouse.

"I'd imagine it would be one of the most remote recording projects happening in the world right now," Ivin said.

"It's very hard to say, there's lots of variable definitions of that, but I would say that's not a stretch."

The band members gathered around a campfire at Ilkurlka during their recording sessions. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

Ivin helped produce The Desert Stars's second album, which was recorded in 2016 at Wingellina in the Indigenous-owned studios of NG Media.

The songs for the third album were recorded in a less traditional acoustic environment, inside a large steel shed normally used to store machinery at Ilkurka.

Ivin said it added to the album's authenticity, despite the fact recording had to be suspended several times due to rain on the tin roof.

"We're not in some slick studio where everything is controlled, or a sterile environment," he said.

The band's set list for rehearsals in the shed. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

"We're in quite an authentic environment, where you can step outside and walk straight back into the desert again.

"Sometimes we opened the doors and looked at the view. If it's a nice, still day, we would open the doors and let the sun in, and it's a natural way to do it.

"It does sound better than you'd think it would [in a shed]."

Lead guitarist Desmond Anderson echoed those sentiments.

"It's pretty peaceful, had a good feeling and good to be back on country where my elders walked ... it's a privilege and an honour," he said.

"It definitely [comes across in the recording], just beautiful."

Desmond Anderson is lead guitarist for The Desert Stars. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

De facto manager

For Ian Baird, who has been involved with the band since 2003 and acted as a de facto manager, The Desert Stars's connection to country has never been in doubt.

Baird recalled how Minning was a natural performer, having made himself a makeshift stage as a child at Cundelee, while it was his father who carved him his first guitar out of wood.

He said they faced ongoing challenges interacting with the mainstream.

The Desert Stars on country near Tjuntjuntjarra (from left) Ashley Frances, Justin Currie, James Minning and Desmond Anderson. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

"This is their country, they were invaded and they are pretty much treated like second-class citizens ... refugees in their own country," he said.

"I think they invented the word resilience. It throws back to pre-contact days.

"You had to be strong, resilient, knowledgeable about country ... because life in the desert with little food and water was all about survival.

Loading...

"We have these artistic talents that the outside world often don't know about, and they've got something to offer."

With most members of The Desert Stars now in their mid to late 40s, the band is evolving again.

"It's a blast for me to perform live. It's a childhood dream," Anderson said.

"It's really good to play on country ... we're tribal people."

The Desert Stars expect their third album to be released next year. (Supplied: Desert Stars)

And on the occasion when an audience knows the words to a song written by Minning?

"There's no words to explain that, it's just a smile ... seeing that is good because someone got the message," he said.

"We're not the only Aboriginal band out there. People in the cities don't realise there's a lot of rock 'n' roll bands out there ... if they get the chance then they will see how much talent they've got at a young age."

title: Work starts on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years
text:
It has taken two decades, but Bundaberg's next hotel development is underway.

Four hours north of Brisbane, the city is a key tourism destination for the southern Great Barrier Reef but has not attracted significant short-term accommodation development in 20 years, according to Bundaberg Regional Council.

The 4.5-star, three-storey hotel, situated across the road from the Bundaberg Airport, will offer 97 rooms.

Mayor Helen Blackburn said the demand for accommodation was constantly growing.

"The hotel demand study showed us that we were 800 beds short every night in our region," she said.

"This is just one step towards bridging that gap."

Cr Blackburn said it had been difficult to attract hotel developers to the region due to the current stock of aging motels.

"Those older motels sell their rooms at a cheaper rate, which then doesn't give investors the confidence to think that if they build a new hotel, they can get the price for the rooms that they need," she said.

Developer MVP said the new hotel would refresh the hospitality offering in Bundaberg.

"We hope that it will be a destination of choice for travellers to the region and will bring more travellers to the region," a spokesperson said.

Construction is due to finish by the middle of next year. (Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council)

The hotel has been funded by investor MyState Limited, with chief executive Brett Morgan saying the demand was clear.

"Every time you go down the street in Bundaberg, there's no-vacancy signs everywhere," he said.

Mr Morgan said the hotel would also create about 50 ongoing jobs.

Hopes for more operators, airlines

Bundaberg Tourism chief executive Duncan Littler said the development would cater to leisure and business travellers.

"Already, there's more than 750,000 people that choose to visit the beautiful Bundaberg region each year and they stay for more than 2 million nights," he said.

"We hope that investments like this will also encourage other [tourism] operators, potentially even airlines, to consider investing in the region."

Brett Morgan, Helen Blackburn and Duncan Littler have welcomed the project. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

Cr Blackburn said other accommodation applications were in the pipeline but did not elaborate.

"We have definitely been encouraging accommodation providers in terms of hotels, student accommodation and even aged care accommodation to set up in our region because we know that we need that here," she said.

Construction on the Airport Drive hotel is due to finish by mid-2027, with the first guests expected later next year.

title: Live: Wallaroos thrash Scotland 56-12 ahead of Wallabies' clash with All Blacks
text:
The Wallaroos have scored a massive 56-12 win to open rugby's historic quadruple header at Stadium Australia, before the Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the Bledisloe Cup.

It is the Wallaroos' second straight win over the Scots, and they will meet again in Canberra on Friday night.

Meanwhile, the Australian women's sevens team fell to their trans-Tasman rivals.

New Zealand won the preseason match against the world champions, 21-12.

In the men's sevens match, Australia drew 19-19 with Fiji.

It is the first time all four of Australia's national teams have appeared on the same match-day schedule.

title: 'Decision next year': Nawaqanitawase keeps Wallabies options open
text:
Mark Nawaqanitawase is refusing to rule out turning his back on Australia for next year's home Rugby World Cup as a three-nation tug-of-war for the cross-code super talent escalates.

While Wallabies captain Harry Wilson and coach Les Kiss have no doubts Nawaqanitawase will be wearing the gold jumper at the 2027 global showpiece, the player himself is keeping his options open.

The in-demand winger's manager this week suggested Nawaqanitawase may choose to represent Fiji, to honour his father's heritage, or Italy, who the dual international is also eligible for through his grandmother.

Still only 26, the prospect of Nawaqanitawase defecting from Australia had seemed improbable.

Under World Rugby laws, if he chose to switch allegiances, following 11 Test appearances for Australia in 2022-23 before enjoying a hugely successful two-year stint in the NRL, the dual international would not be allowed to wear the Wallabies jumper ever again.

Wallabies in awe of Nawaqanitawase It was not just the 80,000 spectators, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Representing Fiji or Italy could appear a more appealing scenario in the twilight of his career, but not his pomp.

However, the newly-crowned NRL premiership winner took to social media yesterday to reveal he had yet to make any decisions about his playing future beyond a looming two-year, $3 million stint in Japan under former Wallabies coach Robbie Deans.

"I just thought I would jump on here as there has been a lot of speculation on my future," Nawaqanitawase posted on Instagram.

"My only focus right now is moving to Japan in a couple of weeks and connecting with my new team at Saitama Wild Knights.

"I will weigh up my options and make a decision next year on my international future.

"Love, Marky."

After taking in the Kangaroos' thrilling Rugby League World Cup win over New Zealand on Thursday night with Nawaqanitawase in Sydney, Wilson is confident the free agent will be playing for Australia next year.

"I don't have to convince him," Wilson said ahead of the Wallabies' second Bledisloe Cup clash with the All Blacks in Sydney today.

" I played junior Wallabies with him, played Wallabies with him, saw him last night supporting the Kangaroos, so I think it's pretty obvious who he wants to play for. "

Coach Kiss is also optimistic about the 2023 Olympic sevens star opting for a Wallabies return next year.

"I think there's no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure," Kiss said.

"We'll continue our conversations and go from there. I'm not going to speak on his behalf at all. But we know where he wants to play."

AAP

title: Hail, fallen trees and blackouts couldn't stop Alice Springs Masters Games
text:
The skies opened, trees fell and sporting competitions ground to a halt, but the spirit of the Alice Springs Masters Games proved difficult to dampen as it marked its 40th anniversary amid rain, hail and destructive winds.

The first hailstones fell on Friday last week, a day before the Games began, and by Monday a destructive storm had swept through the town, bringing down powerlines, damaging homes and leaving about 9,000 properties without electricity.



The weather forced the cancellation of Tuesday's golf competition and Wednesday's street party was moved indoors to the Alice Springs Convention Centre.

Tim Henderson says his wife won six gold medals in swimming events at this year's Games. (ABC Alice Springs: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick)

Among the 1,800 athletes competing in more than 20 sports over the week was Masters veteran Tim Henderson, who said he had never experienced an event quite like it.

"Extraordinary weather, you know — massive hailstones and really strong winds and pulling down lots of trees," he said.

"So the Tuesday round was cancelled. I think I spent most of the day with the chainsaw."

Hail the size of golf balls fell at Lyndavale Station south west of Alice Springs. (Supplied: Ross Stanes)





The community came together to clear the golf course. (ABC Alice Springs: Chris Murrkarany Fitzpatrick) Another storm interrupted Wednesday's golf competition for about an hour, but the conditions on the green were fairer on Thursday.

Henderson said competitors were determined to carry on.

"You want to try and keep it going if you can — it's such a great event," he said.

"It just brings a whole load of people into town [who] have a great time and realise how amazing Alice is."

Long-time competitor Margaret Roberts was a teacher in remote Northern Territory communities. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

More than medals

For veteran swimmer Margaret Roberts, who turns 89 next month, the weather brought a different kind of challenge.

"The wind was blowing and the next thing ice started coming in as well," she said.



Roberts feared the swimming events would be cancelled, but organisers managed to get them back underway.

Andrew Hogg competed in several running events, including a half marathon and two 6-kilometre trail races. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Gosford athlete Andrew Hogg, who claimed victory in the Masters Mile on Wednesday, said the response from residents to the storms left an impression.

"Everybody out on the streets with chainsaws, saws," he said.

"If anybody's got any question about Alice and the community, they just got to see what happened on Monday night."

Trees pulled down powerlines across Alice Springs after Monday's severe storm. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

As the Games draw to a close, competitors are reflecting on a week defined as much by resilience and community spirit as by sporting achievements.

For Roberts, who has been competing for decades, the event has always been about friendship, competition and staying active.

"Keep moving," she said.

"Don't sit down and rock."

After a week spent stopping, recovering and starting again, her advice seems fitting.

title: Darwin accountant trades tax for cane toad taxidermy
text:
There are 531 dead cane toads in Mithram Selvaratnam's Darwin backyard freezers.

By Christmas, some will be wearing Santa hats.

The former accountant runs an unusual souvenir business, which sees him doing everything from sandblasting and whitening crocodile skulls to gutting and stuffing dead toads.

Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam now sells taxidermy cane toads and crocodile products at Darwin's markets. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

It's a far cry from the life he envisioned for himself when he left Malaysia to study accounting in Australia 16 years ago.

"When I grew up it was all about the rat race," he said.

" There was no way this was part of my five or 10-year plan, that's for sure. "

The decision to leave it all behind came to Mr Selvaratnam after working full time as an accountant in Melbourne.

"I was doing that corporate life, 9 to 5, stuck in the office, and I just felt like there was more to life," he said.

Christmas-themed cane toads are being prepared for the festive season. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

Word of Mr Selvaratnam's dilemma got out to his Darwin-based aunt, who offered an unexpected solution.

For decades she had been selling curries at the iconic Mindil Markets and a neighbouring stall had put his Territory souvenir business up for sale.

Taxidermy bootcamp

That was in 2017 and the transition from spreadsheets to stuffed toads hasn't always been smooth sailing.

Mr Selvaratnam was initially purchasing the toads from a taxidermist in Queensland, but when the supplier decided to retire, he was left with two choices — give up the business or take matters into his own hands.

Grace Ray works on a taxidermy cane toad at Mithram's Leanyer work space. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

"Before I started doing this, I could barely pick a toad up," he said.

"But I thought, we have plenty of toads in the Territory, an abundance of supply, so I'll just make them myself.

"I went [to Townsville] and put myself through a two-day bootcamp of learning how to do it."

It was through gritted teeth and pinched nostrils that Mr Selvaratnam learnt to gut, tan, stuff and dry the warty pests before painting them with varnish to make them "look pretty".

Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam couldn't even touch cane toads until he underwent 'taxidermy bootcamp'. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

Armed with his new-found knowledge, a head torch and gloves, Mr Selvaratnam began scouring golf courses and gardens hunting the pests.

Until he hit the jackpot.

Toad busters

Community 'toad busts', like the one held recently at the Territory Wildlife Park, can provide hundreds of dead toads to Mr Selvaratnam in a single night without him having to lift a finger.

Territory Wildlife Park ranger Luke Hare says toad busts aim to reduce the numbers of the pests while also educating the community of their dangers.

"Cane toads produce significant risk to a lot of our native species," he said.

"A lot of our natives can't tolerate the toxins cane toads have, so when they eat the cane toad, or try to eat them, often it will kill them."

Mr Hare estimates that there could be hundreds of thousands of cane toads running rampant in the wildlife park on Darwin's outskirts.

For Mr Selvaratnam, the park's latest haul of 531 toads has come just in time for his end-of-year Christmas orders.

Soon, newly minted santa hat-clad critters will join their rum-drinking, ukulele-playing and occasionally X-rated counterparts.

The recent toad bust has filled the freezers at his Leanyer workshop. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

A second life

But cane toads aren't the only unwanted creatures finding a second life in Mr Selvaratnam's backyard.

Among the tanning equipment and taxidermy tools are chest freezers full of crocodile heads.

"I started with the toads and the skulls came about a year after that," he said.

Crocodile teeth and skulls are also turned into souvenirs. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

Mr Selvaratnam had initially been buying the skulls from a supplier, but in a case of deja vu, retirement once again threatened his supply chain.

"This time I didn't go down to Queensland to learn, I just got him on the phone and he ran me through it, and from then, on experimentation, really," he said.

The skulls are a by-product from crocodile farms in the Territory, and along with croc teeth, buffalo heads and other leather goods, they make up the rest of Mr Selvaratnam's unlikely livelihood.

He's also recently been experimenting with other forms of taxidermy including the Territory's iconic barramundi.

Mithram Selvaratnam has been testing out his taxidermy skills on barramundi. (ABC News: Lillian Watkins)

"It's stuff that is quite different, things that people normally just throw away, there's no other use for heads and carcasses," he said.

"So being able to give them a second life, it's nice."

title: Restored cottage gives insight into life on Snowy Scheme
text:
Finding accommodation for workers on major infrastructure projects might seem like a thoroughly modern problem, but history shows that is not the case.

When work on the Snowy Scheme began more than 75 years ago, about 200 portable timber cottages were needed to house workers and their families.

One of those structures has now gone on display at the Snowy Scheme Museum in Adaminaby.

It gives visitors an insight into the extraordinarily transient life of those on the front lines of Australia's largest engineering project.

The refurbished cottage has been fitted to resemble life on the Snowy Scheme. (Supplied: Snowy Scheme Museum)

Museum president Tim Corkill said the cottages were important because the scheme was built in stages across different areas, with workers living in various temporary towns.

"You might have started off in Tantangara in the morning and in the afternoon you ended up in Island Bend," he said.

Mr Corkill said the two and three-bedroom cottages were designed for families and trucked from town to town, often with everything inside.

"The wardrobes were full and the kitchen was full, and all the furniture," he said.

The transportable cottages housed workers and families on the Snowy Scheme in the 1950s and 60s. (Supplied: Snowy Scheme Museum)

"They needed to ... move a lot of houses in and all the other infrastructure in to establish the town sites," he said.

"When that particular project finished, they then moved onto another site, another township."

The cottages were often transported with household items inside. (Supplied: Snowy Scheme Museum)

Keeping out the cold

Mr Corkhill said the cottages were not "super warm" but gave some protection against harsh winters, with wood heaters, double glazing, and insulation in the ceilings, walls and floors.

Staying warm was essential, with one temporary town, Happy Jacks, the highest in Australia at the time, almost 1,500 metres above sea level.

"The kids went to school there on skis and they had absolutely fond memories," Mr Corkill said.

Tim Corkill is eager to welcome visitors to the cottage. (ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams)

Bringing the cottage to the museum was a challenge.

"The easy part was moving it. The more complicated part was actually organising it," Mr Corkill said.

"Once we got the approvals, we were actually able to move the house from near Nimmitabel … within the day."

These designs show plans for the Snowy cottages. (Supplied: Snowy Scheme Museum)

The two-bedroom cottage is just under 4 metres wide and about 12 metres long, and less garish than others of the era.

"They were painted anything from orange to pinks to light blues to greens," Mr Corkill said.

"Against the white backdrop of snow ... they would have stood out."

Colourful homes dotted the horizon in the township of Cabramurra. (Supplied: Snowy Scheme Museum)

Where are they now?

When the Snowy Scheme was finished, the cottages were sold.

Mr Corkhill said they ended up scattered around the region, often used as farm sheds or holiday homes on the New South Wales far south coast.

Other cottages had already been on the coast for decades, giving Snowy workers a place to relax.

Joe Werner's father was one of five German engineers charged with ensuring tunnel ends met in the middle.

When Norwegian contractor Selma finished working on the scheme's Guthega project, the Werners bought one of its cottages and erected it on the coast at Pambula.

"They were only sort of temporary buildings, but they functioned very well," Mr Werner said.

"It was good enough for a holiday cottage and that's what my father bought it for."

The Werner family turned a workers' cottage into a beachside holiday home. (Supplied: Joe Werner)

Mr Werner's father faced issues with council regulations, but Snowy Mountains Authority commissioner William Hudson intervened.

"Sir William wrote to the mayor saying, 'Look, our top Snowy personnel work very hard under very difficult situations. They need rest and recreation. Can you just overlook these little issues so that they can get some rest,' and the mayor agreed," Mr Werner said.

"We had unobstructed ocean views.

" We thought it was heaven. "

Mr Werner said it was common for Snowy workers to holiday on the coast "because it was so convenient".

Sir William's daughter Anne and her husband even honeymooned in the cottage.

The family sold in 1972, but the building remains.

"That's the astonishing thing," Mr Werner said.

"They weren't built to last.

"It's amazing that so many of them have."

title: Final race meet marks end of nights out at 'Wenty'
text:
For 94 years a night out at the dogs at Wenty, as it's known to locals, has been a Sydney institution.

A sell-out crowd turned out to witness the end of an era as the starting gates rose for the final time, marking the end of greyhound racing at Wentworth Park.

Dog owners, trainers and punters turned out for the final event. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

For many dog owners, trainers and punters, it was a night tinged with sadness and nostalgia.

"I'm been coming here with my mother and father since I was eight-years-old, so I have got to come for the last night," trainer Ron Marsden said.

"Sad to see it go especially as I don't live that far away."

A race during the final Million Dollar Chase greyhound race at Wentworth Park Stadium. (AAP: Robbie Stephenson)

John Hill from Orange, part-owner of a dog called Fearless Bandit running in the final race, the Million Dollar Chase, said he had been coming to the track for 45 years.

"It's a bit of a shame, it's been here for 90-odd years," he said.

" It's an iconic track, it's just got a sound and a ring to it that no other track has got in Australia so very, very sad to see it go. "

John Hill describes Wentworth Park as an "iconic track". (ABC News)

Arriving at the turnstiles, the 6,000 ticket holders were greeted by a jubilant collection of animal rights protesters who gathered in a park across the road to celebrate the occasion.

"We are here to say good riddance to greyhound racing in the city," Greens MP Kobi Shetty said.

"We want to see greyhound racing shut down for good so this is a step in the right direction."

Protesters say the closure of the track is a "win for the greyhounds". (ABC News: Ursula Malone)

Protester John Papanidis said the closure of Wentworth Park was a huge victory for campaigners.

"This is the jewel in the crown of the racing industry," he said.

"They're trying to celebrate tonight, but it's a huge loss for them and a win for the greyhounds."

Inside, a blast of trumpet over the loudspeakers was the cue for trainers to file into the parade enclosure, leading dogs muzzled and draped in their racing colours.

'Night out at the dogs at Wenty'

Early races, after the track's opening in 1932, were held on the grass. (Supplied)

Greyhound racing started at Wentworth Park in October 1932.

Early races were held on the grass before a track with a mechanical tin hare was constructed in 1939 at a cost of 33,000 pounds.

A "night out at the dogs at Wenty" soon became a Sydney institution, with crowds as big as 15,000 people crammed into the Glebe racetrack on a Saturday night, jostling for a glimpse of champion dogs such as Qualinor, Zoom Top and Farraflash.

Zoom Top was among the greyhounds that attracted crowds in the track's heyday. (Supplied: Greyhound Journal)

In the betting ring, bookmakers shouted out the odds, depositing cash in the heavy leather bags strung around their neck.

"It was part of the working class culture of the area," Max Solling, historian and author of Going to the Dogs: A History of Greyhound Racing in NSW told the ABC.

"People were coming here to hope that they're going to win something on the dogs, fame or riches even better.

"Very few ever succeeded."

Max Solling says that going to the greyhound races was "part of the working class culture of the area". (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

By the 1960s, the crowds at Wentworth Park had dwindled to a few hundred with the advent of off-track betting.

"The decline of attendance is wholly due to the TAB," Mr Solling said.

"The attendance spiralled down and stayed down, never recovered. You would be lucky to have 500 people here because it's all online."

The rise of off-track betting had a big impact on attendance. (State Library of NSW: Ern McQuillan)

A ban and a reversal

In July 2016, following a scandal over allegations of animal cruelty in the sport, then NSW premier Mike Baird announced a ban on greyhound racing in the state from July 2017.

The announcement sparked a fierce backlash from the industry and its supporters on both sides of politics.

Hundreds of protesters joining what was dubbed the Fair Go Rally, marching on Parliament House in Macquarie Street to demand the ban be overturned.

The decision in 2016 to ban greyhound racing sparked a backlash and protests. (Supplied: Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party)

Three months later, with his approval ratings in decline, the premier reversed his decision, agreeing to give the sport "one last chance", and allocating $41 million in government money to fund the reforms.

According to Mr Solling, the debate over animal cruelty in greyhound racing gave rise to accusations of double standards when it came to the treatment of horse racing.

"It's clearly about class," he said.

"They're not going to close down the Melbourne Cup, why do they do it to the dogs?"

Plans for new home

Then in July this year came yet another surprise announcement.

With its lease at Wentworth Park not set to expire until September 2027, the Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association revealed it was opting to vacate the site a year early.

"The venue no longer suited our participants who are largely located outside the Sydney basin," Greyhound Racing NSW CEO Steve Griffin said at the time.

The Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association opted to terminate its lease a year before it expired. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

For now, racing will shift to Gosford on the Central Coast, but Greyhound Racing NSW has announced a longer term plan for a move to Richmond, in Sydney's north-west, following an upgrade of the existing facilities there.

"The new Sydney Metropolitan Racing Precinct, once constructed, will also secure the industry's financial future with revenue coming into the sport from greater use of the facility," Mr Griffin said.

"Additionally, unlike Wenty, we own the site so can never be removed from it, which is a great position for the sport to be in."

At the same time, the racing club at Wentworth Park, the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association, announced this week it was looking at a site near Appin, in south-west Sydney.

An artist's impression of the Richmond site to house the new Sydney Metropolitan Racing Precinct. (Supplied: Greyhound Racing NSW)

Whichever option eventuates, the NSW government has promised $10 million in government funding to help with the transition.

"We are disappointed the government is spending $10 million to relocate racing to some other location from here," Ms Shetty said.

"We think it's time to just call it on greyhound racing, and that $10 million could have been spent elsewhere."

The racetrack at Wentworth Park is now set to be demolished with the Crown land transferred to the City of Sydney Council.

Kobi Shetty says she is disappointed the NSW government has promised $10 million to help the industry with the transition. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The plan is for the site to be converted into sports fields and parkland for public use.

"We know that Ultimo and Pyrmont are two of the most densely populated suburbs in Australia so there is a desperate need for more places for people to play," Ms Shetty said.

Work on the demolition of the grandstand, built at great cost in 1987, is expected to start before Christmas.

title: Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs
text:

Investigation NationalNSWCity life Whose club is it anyway? The battle over one of Sydney’s largest football clubs Max Maddison October 17, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Herb Greedy Hall in Marrickville echoed with hissing and howling. Members of Marrickville FC – one of the largest community football clubs in Australia – had arrived in their hundreds for an annual general meeting in early December. It was an amazing turnout given only 15 people had attended the AGM 10 months earlier. The Marrickville Red Devils. Marrickville FC A faction of parents and coaches had become quietly, then vocally, concerned about the direction of the Red Devils, as the club is affectionately known. Together, they established Marrickville Community Voice, a group of members whom they hoped would be elected onto the club’s board. The club had transformed from a community organisation into a commercial enterprise where money was the primary issue, one parent involved alleged later. A notable shift in the culture was evident in the inclusion of bonus performance payments for some junior coaches in 2026, claimed two parents.

Advertisement

But after the breakaway faction’s plans became known, supporters of the club’s president Bill Drossos and the management committee rallied, turning out in force to stop what they alleged was an attempt to “overthrow the board”. The meeting ran for 80 minutes and, at times, had the decorum of a boxing match. It would rank among the more controversial days in the club’s 80-year history. Seven parents, former coaches and members spoke to this masthead as part of this story. All except one did so on the condition of anonymity to protect relationships. There were questions at the AGM about an alleged lack of transparency about the club’s finances, such as why the commercial terms of a five-a-side competition, run as a joint venture between Marrickville and a company owned by Drossos, appeared shrouded in secrecy? Aside from the question of finances, the crux of the disagreement was a dispute over the soul of a community football club. Who should a sporting club be run for? And how much should winning be valued in children’s sport?

Advertisement

It is a microcosm of the modern era: one where more is understood about the cost of prioritising results in children’s football over enjoyment, but where high-performance football squads have proliferated as intensely involved parents, living vicariously through their kids, have pushed them to succeed. Related Article Sports science Injuries, burnout, huge bills: Are pushy parents ruining children’s sport? Culture Tom Engesser, the former technical director of Marrickville FC, personified one of the competing philosophies of coaching children’s sport. “If something didn’t come off, I had heard him say, ‘Wow that was a really good idea; it may not have come off because your skills don’t match your thinking’,” says a mother who was involved in her son’s Red Devils side.

Advertisement

“It wasn’t about winning. He encouraged them to take risks.” According to coaches and parents at Marrickville FC, the technical director took a high-level view on coaching. In a game as chaotic and error-prone as children’s football, the obvious temptation is risk mitigation: playing direct and punting the ball long – hopefully to one or two strong, fast and gifted players who score all your goals. Engesser’s approach was different – encouraging players to play more like Spain; passing and controlling possession which invariably causes mistakes. The cost can be short-term results. But the upshot is the development of players, who become infinitely better as they learn by making mistakes. When coaches emphasise outcomes, the risk is young players become trapped in a mentality that success is a precondition of involvement. In contrast, Engesser wanted players to be better thinking footballers and enjoy the game for enjoyment’s sake.

Advertisement

He was constantly telling people the peak dropout period for boys in football was when they turned 14 – the age when they realised they wouldn’t make it professionally, the mother says. “Some parents thought he wasn’t focused enough on winning,” she says. “But he wanted to keep as many kids in the game as possible.” Then he was gone. A post on Marrickville FC’s Facebook account in June last year notified members that Engesser, who had recently finished coaching the club’s first grade side, had decided after 17 years at the club, he would step down “effective immediately”. The announcement generated an outpouring of support for Engesser. “A huge loss for our club and all our players, get him back ASAP before another club grabs him,” read one post underneath the Facebook post. Engesser declined to comment.

Advertisement

Not only did Engesser depart, but evidence of a new coaching philosophy emerged. Obtained by this masthead, a contract for junior selective development coaches for the most recent winter season stipulates bonus payments would be triggered by various successes: $250 for finishing first, $250 for semi-final qualification, and $500 for a grand final win. “Balance player improvement and development with an equal focus on team and match-based success culminating in semi-final qualifications and a grand final championship,” reads a key performance indicator in the contract. Marrickville FC managing director Georgina Kokokiris told this masthead that Engesser had left of his own accord, saying the club offered to expand his role and his departure had “absolutely nothing to do with coaching philosophy”.

Advertisement

She said a “very small percentage” of the club’s teams were coached by paid accredited coaches, and those agreements were commercial in confidence. There were “many aspects in these agreements”, and the club had the “right balance of individual development and support of our juniors”, Kokokiris said. Finances On the blustery first evening of last December, Adam Smith entered the AGM with a list of seemingly straightforward questions he believed the club’s leadership should answer about its finances. Adam Smith, a Marrickville FC parent and club member, asked the club for greater financial transparency. Jessica Hromas Smith – a club member and parent with no involvement in the Marrickville Community Voice – held two main concerns: the club’s qualified audit opinion, and the summer five-a-side competition, a commercial relationship between Marrickville FC and Sportzology, a sports uniform supplier owned by Drossos and his wife.

Advertisement

The 50-50 profit-sharing joint venture had grown rapidly since being established in 2018, to now include 250 teams. Drossos told the AGM that Sportzology had invested a “lot of money” to build and design the program, which included the naming rights, website and intellectual property. Moreover, the agreement was established before he joined the club and the contract had been renewed the previous year at “arm’s length”, he said. Yet, when Smith asked if the terms of the contract would be made available, or even the dollar amount Sportzology earned be made public, Drossos demurred, saying: “It’s a commercial arrangement.” In comments to this masthead, Smith said he was surprised his questions at the AGM about the accounts were taken as an attack on the club. “It has grown from a volunteer-run community club into a $1.8 million operation, mostly from families’ registration, with paid staff,” he said. “The governance hasn’t kept up with the money. “At that size, an arrangement with a company connected to the president should be set out in the accounts. There is no related party note in them at all.”

Advertisement

In comments to this masthead, Drossos said the club had thousands of members and only one had requested access to the information. “Marrickville FC have many agreements with related party organisations including former and current management committee members and copies of these agreements and arrangements as you would expect are commercial in confidence,” he said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Government grants The football club that used taxpayer grant for coach and player wages, wine and pub meals Kokokiris denied the club had not disclosed details of the arrangement with Sportzology, which she said had been “independently approved” by the current board. Drossos had brought a “wealth of experience, large fundraising, and additional revenue streams” to the club, she said. “This has allowed us to invest back into our club and its members including keeping our community registration fees as low as possible and not increasing those community registration fees for the past three years,” she said.

Advertisement

For the past six years, Drossos has been head of partnerships at the Macarthur FC, home to the Bulls, an A-League franchise based in south-western Sydney. When it came time for questions, an already tense meeting turned ugly. Supporters of the existing management committee alleged the Marrickville Community Voice “breached privacy” by obtaining a list of parents’ emails to send them information about their plans without their consent. As the meeting ticked over an hour, club legend Ron Royston was asked to deliver his verdict on the board’s performance. The 70-year club veteran, revelling in Marrickville FC’s 183 winter teams, proclaimed the already good club was only going to get better, but offered a warning. To see so many people at the meeting was “brilliant”, he said. “But I’m just hoping you’ve been here for the right bloody reason, not to disrupt this club.” Whether heeding Royston’s advice or not, the Marrickville Community Voice disbanded. Ten months later, Smith says he is still waiting for answers.

text:

Buenos Aires: At first, there was nothing unusual about Celia Melamed’s new client. His English mastiff was dying, so he hired her to read its mind. But when she met the man with the messy hair, he kept apologising for his casual outfit. “He told me, ‘Sorry for being dressed like this; I’m always in a suit on television’,” Melamed recalled. “I don’t have a television, so I had no idea what he was talking about.” The man was Javier Milei, at the time a TV pundit in Argentina known for railing against the government. The mastiff was Conan, soon to be Argentina’s most famous dog. And Melamed, by extension, was about to become the nation’s most well-known animal psychic. Celia Melamed says Javier Milei, pictured, hired her to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. Marcelo Dubini/Caras via The New York Times That is because, a few years later, Milei was elected Argentina’s president, and Conan was a symbol of his brash campaign, as well as the genetic model for the handful of clones that are now the nation’s first dogs.

Advertisement

But in that first encounter about a decade ago, Conan was on his deathbed, and Melamed said she was communicating with him via an energy she felt in her chest. She said she relayed Milei’s message that he was desperately trying to save the dog. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Trump spends America’s billions to save a friend in need Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “What I remember is that he felt better afterwards,” she said of Milei. “Few people have such an intense connection with their animals.” Melamed then became his dedicated pet psychic. He kept hiring her for the next two years, she said, including to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. They stopped working together a few years before Milei was elected president in 2023. Milei and his spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment. He has long made clear that he views his dogs as more than just pets. Milei, who is unmarried and childless, refers to them as his children, and his press secretary has admonished reporters who ask about the animals, saying it is equivalent to snooping into his family.

Advertisement

As a result, the dogs have become a central mystery of Milei’s presidency. Only one has been seen publicly since he was elected president, and there have been frequent rumours that others have died. When Milei suddenly fired much of the presidential residence’s staff last month, Argentine pundits speculated the move had something to do with his dogs, which he has said are kept in separate kennels there. It has even become common political fodder in Argentina that Milei seeks out his dogs for advice. A top foreign diplomat and a long-time friend of Milei’s, both of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said they have heard Milei say so. Celia Melamed charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times When asked by journalists about the claim, Milei has responded coyly, saying what happens in his house is private. “If he gives me advice, he’s a genius,” Milei said in 2023, referring to Conan. (Although Conan died in 2017, Milei has suggested that one of the clones is Conan’s reincarnation.) Asked whether she delivered a dog’s counsel to the future president, Melamed cited client privacy.

Advertisement

Milei was hardly her only client. After her work for him became public a few years ago, her waitlist ballooned to two months, she said. From her tiny Buenos Aires apartment draped in wind chimes and dream catchers, Melamed, 67, charges pet owners $US35 ($50) an hour to communicate with their dogs, cats, turtles and birds to find out what is ailing the animals, where they are hiding or how they are doing in the afterlife. She says she needs merely a photo of an animal to perceive its emotions and thoughts, typically via sensations in her body. Loading “How does it work?” she said. “I don’t know. I only know that it works.” She represents what appears to be increasing global interest in the business of pet telepathy, notwithstanding an absence of scientific evidence.

Advertisement

While there are no reliable statistics on the industry, self-proclaimed animal communicators and their clients have proliferated on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram. Popular animal communicators on social media say business is booming. Related Article Protests A nationwide shutdown tests Milei’s tough medicine for Argentina ”When I started out, I was pretty much alone,” said Cindy Brody, a communicator from Woodstock, New York, who has been in the business for nearly 40 years. Interest took off several years ago, she said, and now her waitlist was nearly a month long. She holds up to 20 sessions a week, charging $US275 an hour. “It’s our time now,” she said. Clara Martín, an animal communicator from Madrid, said her clients were also multiplying, including a wild-animal sanctuary in South Africa and a man living with 23 cats in Japan. “People understand their animals have something to say,” she said. Melamed said she first noticed her powerful intuition as a child when she could predict correct answers in guessing games. But she never cultivated those abilities during a career in veterinary medicine and bacteriology. Then, in 2008, she read a book about communicating with animals and began taking courses.

Advertisement

Two years later, a horse she was working with stepped on her, but when she telepathically forgave it, she said her pain went away. “I realised there was something much deeper going on,” she said. Over two visits to her home, I watched Melamed work. (Since the COVID-19 pandemic, she has read animals’ minds remotely.) She looked at photos of cats and dogs, closed her eyes and, according to her, connected with the animals almost instantaneously. Stressed animals could make her body feel tense, she said, while lost pets had made her smell things that provided a clue to their whereabouts. “Sometimes what I feel is difficult to put into words,” she said. “I try to be as reliable as possible.” In one case, she said she asked a dog with persistent diarrhoea if it had a message for its owner. “‘Tell her that I’m not her grandmother’,” Melamed recalled the dog responding. The owner was stunned, she said, and admitted she had called the dog her grandmother’s name because of its gait, but would stop. “From that communication onwards, the dog stopped having bloody diarrhoea,” Melamed said. Clara Quattrucci, 65, said she began booking regular appointments with Melamed two years ago after she helped her cocker spaniel, Mia, recover from the emotional trauma of an attack from another dog. “It honestly blew my mind,” she said.

Advertisement

Dozens of people now advertised pet-psychic services in Buenos Aires, up from just a handful a decade ago, she said. That is in part thanks to Melamed. She estimates she has trained about 700 people in her pet-communication workshops. “We’re all capable,” she said. “The only thing that blocks us is our belief we can’t.” At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover. Sarah Pabst/The New York Times She even taught the person she believes took her place working with Milei’s dogs: the president’s sister. Karina Milei, who is arguably Argentina’s second most powerful government official, showed innate talent in communicating with animals, Melamed said. She took Melamed’s weekend workshop around 2019, and then texted Melamed for months after for more guidance. Shortly after, she said, Javier Milei stopped hiring her.

Advertisement

Karina Milei did not respond to a request for comment. Melamed said she voted for Javier Milei and looks back fondly on their time together. After Conan died, she said Milei hired her to communicate with the dog’s genetic replicas. They were rambunctious puppies, anxious about their new home, she recalled. “They all have different personalities,” she said. “Even though they are all clones.” Milei, a libertarian economist, named four of the five clones after libertarian economists. The fifth he named Conan. It is that dog that Milei says is a reincarnation of his original pet, Melamed said, noting it immediately knew the layout of his house. “I think it’s very likely,” she said. When she communicated with that clone, she added, “there was a feeling of familiarity.” Her endorsement of the theory could mean a lot to Argentina’s president, who seemed to think highly of Melamed’s apparent powers. At Melamed’s apartment, a book written by Milei had a message she said he had scrawled on its inside cover.

Advertisement

“For Celia, TOTAL GENIUS OF THE UNIVERSE,” it said, “the being of light who helped me find the way.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Washington: Ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty told an inquiry it is not Australia’s fault that the American lamb industry is struggling, as the Trump administration considers imposing new tariffs or restrictions on $1.6 billion of sheep meat Australia exports to the US. Moriarty said drought, reduced wool demand and the US government’s removal of wool subsidies were to blame for the longstanding decline in lamb meat production, not the proliferation of cheaper imports from Australia. Australian ambassador to the US Greg Moriarty, pictured with Donald Trump when they met in May. “Imports have filled the supply gap created by this decline in domestic production. They are a consequence of reduced US output, not a substantial cause of it,” he told the US International Trade Commission. “Any action to restrict lamb meat imports would only increase costs for US consumers, reduce product availability and risk reversing the steady growth in US demand for lamb to the detriment of the US industry.”

Advertisement

Moriarty said Australia’s supply of high-quality lamb actually helped develop the US sheep industry, and contributed to flock productivity through genetics partnerships, technology transfer and pest research. Meat has been a source of tension in the US-Australia trade relationship, with President Donald Trump imposing tariffs on beef imports before removing them to combat high consumer prices. Sheep at a farm in Kansas. Parts of the domestic lamb industry have called for import restrictions to help redress a “crisis”. Bloomberg The US imports nearly 80 per cent of the lamb consumed by Americans, with shipments from Australia and New Zealand accounting for “nearly all” of that, according to the commission’s staff report. US Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer instructed the commission to examine whether those imports posed a serious injury to America’s domestic industry – a precursor to new trade barriers such as tariffs or quotas.

Advertisement

At a hearing on Friday (Washington time), the US sheep industry and graziers pushed back against what they called “audacious” testimony from Australia’s government and industry representatives. Paul Rosenthal, a trade lawyer at Kelley Drye & Warren representing the American Sheep Industry Association, argued imports had displaced US producers and caused the decline in domestic production, rather than filled a hole. It was disingenuous to argue otherwise, he said, and “reminiscent of the proverbial story about the boy who killed his parents and threw himself at the mercy of the court because he’s an orphan”. Rosenthal said exporters were attempting to portray a biblical utopia of the lion laying down with the lamb. “This idealised vision of prosperity for the lamb industry conjures visions of the peaceable kingdom – a common place where all God’s creatures will live in harmony,” he said. “As we all know, we have not achieved that peace on earth, and certainly not in the domestic sheep industry.”

Advertisement

But Moriarty and Australian industry representatives pointed to multiple periods over the past 30 years in which both imports and domestic production of lamb fell at the same time. Related Article Exclusive

Trade ‘Fill the gap’: Australia’s plan to swoop on Trump’s trade war with Canada “This demonstrates that domestic production does not improve even where there are fewer imports,” Australia’s ambassador said. Matthew Nicely, a trade lawyer at Akin Gump, representing Meat & Livestock Australia, noted most American producers surveyed by the commission did not call for more trade barriers. Of the 49 who responded, 31 did not report injury from imports and took no position on relief measures. Meanwhile, US lamb prices have recently surged to historic highs, while Australian exports to the US have fallen amid drought – a decline projected to continue until the end of 2027, Moriarty told the hearing.

Advertisement

Nicely accused companies in favour of tariffs and quotas of using “legal acrobatics” to justify their case, such as redefining the domestic industry to include lamb growers and feeders. Today’s inquiry is similar to one conducted in 1999 when the commission found imports were injuring the US domestic industry and then-president Bill Clinton approved tariffs on Australian exports. Chefs prepare KS7, claimed to be the world’s first 7%+ marbling brand in lamb, at Meat and Livestock Australia. Sitthixay Ditthavong Australia challenged the decision at the World Trade Organisation and won, with the then-Bush administration removing the tariffs. At that time, imports only accounted for a fifth of US lamb consumption. Advocates for tariffs told the commission that Australia and New Zealand were making the same arguments they did in 1999, and the situation had only worsened dramatically since then.

Advertisement

But Moriarty said Australia and the US now had a free trade agreement, enacted in 2005, which should preclude tariffs on lamb. Americans have historically eschewed sheep meat, but consumption is increasing. The inquiry heard the typical American only eats lamb once a year, and half of all Americans have never eaten lamb. “There is so much opportunity to improve these figures,” said New Zealand’s ambassador to the US, Chris Seed. The commission is due to make its determination by November 13 and then, if necessary, holding a hearing on potential remedies. It will report to Trump by January.
